claim: Flying animals need continual sensory feedback about their body position and orientation for flight control.
source: Flying animals need continual sensory feedback about their body position and orientation for flight control.
evidence: This is a general statement about flight control that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: The visual system provides essential but slow feedback for flight control.
source: The visual system provides essential but slow feedback.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about visual processing speeds and is referenced throughout the manuscript with citations.

claim: Mechanosensory channels can provide feedback at much shorter timescales than vision.
source: In contrast, mechanosensory channels can provide feedback at much shorter timescales.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about mechanosensory transduction speeds.

claim: In Diptera, fast mechanosensory feedback is provided by organs called halteres.
source: In Diptera, fast mechanosensory feedback is provided by organs called halteres and is crucial for the control of rapid flight manoeuvres, while vision controls manoeuvres in lower temporal frequency bands.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about Dipteran flight control and is consistent with citations provided elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Halteres are crucial for the control of rapid flight manoeuvres in Diptera.
source: In Diptera, fast mechanosensory feedback is provided by organs called halteres and is crucial for the control of rapid flight manoeuvres, while vision controls manoeuvres in lower temporal frequency bands.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations about Dipteran flight control.

claim: Vision controls manoeuvres in lower temporal frequency bands in Diptera.
source: In Diptera, fast mechanosensory feedback is provided by organs called halteres and is crucial for the control of rapid flight manoeuvres, while vision controls manoeuvres in lower temporal frequency bands.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations about Dipteran flight control.

claim: Macroglossum stellatarum uses Johnston's organs in their antennae to provide mechanosensory feedback on perturbations in body position.
source: Here, we have investigated the visual-mechanosensory integration in the hawkmoth Macroglossum stellatarum. They represent a large group of insects that use Johnston's organs in their antennae to provide mechanosensory feedback on perturbations in body position.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and findings of the study, as well as citations to previous work.

claim: Antennal mechanosensory feedback specifically mediates fast flight manoeuvres in Macroglossum stellatarum.
source: Our experiments show that antennal mechanosensory feedback specifically mediates fast flight manoeuvres, but not slow ones.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Antennal mechanosensory feedback does not mediate slow flight manoeuvres in Macroglossum stellatarum.
source: Our experiments show that antennal mechanosensory feedback specifically mediates fast flight manoeuvres, but not slow ones.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data showing that ablated moths could track slow movements similarly to control moths.

claim: There are no compensatory interactions between antennal and visual feedback in Macroglossum stellatarum.
source: Moreover, we did not observe compensatory interactions between antennal and visual feedback.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that light intensity effects were similar across all antennal conditions (Figure 4).

claim: Visual feedback provides key information about flight parameters including ground speed, distance to obstacles and targets, and aerial displacements.
source: Visual feedback provides key information about flight parameters including ground speed, distance to obstacles and targets, and aerial displacements (for a review see Srinivasan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Visual estimation of self-motion is limited by its temporal resolution and substantial latency to flight muscle activation.
source: However, visual estimation of self-motion (Fuller et al., 2014; Hung et al., 2013) is limited by its temporal resolution and substantial latency to flight muscle activation (Sherman and Dickinson, 2004; Suver et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Visual feedback may be too slow to control very fast aerial manoeuvres.
source: This may often be too slow to control very fast aerial manoeuvres, which require rapid sensory feedback before perturbations become uncontrollably large and thus energetically costly to the animals (Bender and Dickinson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and logical inference from the temporal limitations of vision.

claim: Insects use mechanosensors to sense their own motion to avoid the temporal limitations of the visual system.
source: Avoiding the temporal limitations set by the visual system, insects use mechanosensors to sense their own motion, as these can transduce perturbations on much faster time scales (Yarger and Fox, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and established knowledge about mechanosensory transduction.

claim: Mechanosensors can transduce perturbations on much faster time scales than vision.
source: Avoiding the temporal limitations set by the visual system, insects use mechanosensors to sense their own motion, as these can transduce perturbations on much faster time scales (Yarger and Fox, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and established knowledge about mechanosensory physiology.

claim: Halteres of Dipteran insects are a classic example of gyroscopic function in active flight.
source: The halteres of Dipteran insects are a classic example of gyroscopic function in active flight (Fraenkel and Pringle, 1938; Nalbach, 1994; Pringle, 1948).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to classic studies on halteres.

claim: Halteres are club-shaped mechanosensory structures that were evolutionarily derived from the hind-wings.
source: Halteres are club-shaped mechanosensory structures that were evolutionarily derived from the hind-wings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about haltere morphology and evolution.

claim: Halteres vibrate at the wing beat frequency.
source: They vibrate at the wing beat frequency and can sense rotations in any axis, and provide crucial sensory input to stabilise flight after perturbations (Ristroph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and established knowledge about haltere function.

claim: Halteres can sense rotations in any axis.
source: They vibrate at the wing beat frequency and can sense rotations in any axis, and provide crucial sensory input to stabilise flight after perturbations (Ristroph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and established knowledge about haltere function.

claim: Halteres provide crucial sensory input to stabilise flight after perturbations.
source: They vibrate at the wing beat frequency and can sense rotations in any axis, and provide crucial sensory input to stabilise flight after perturbations (Ristroph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Halteres are a special feature of only Dipteran and Strepsipteran insects.
source: Halteres, however, are a special feature of only Dipteran (and Strepsipteran) insects (Pix et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Visual systems of many insects trade off temporal acuity for sensitivity.
source: This question is especially interesting in insects active in dim light, as the visual systems of many insects trade off temporal acuity for sensitivity (Warrant, 1999; Warrant, 2017), thus rendering visually based flight control even less reliable and increasing the need for mechanosensory feedback control.
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on insect vision.

claim: Sphingids are able to fly over a wide range of light intensities due to their superposition compound eyes and additional neural adaptations.
source: Sphingids are a group of flying insects that are able to fly over a wide range of light intensities, due to their superposition compound eyes and additional neural adaptations (O'Carroll et al., 1996; O'Carroll et al., 1997; Stöckl et al., 2017a; Theobald et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on sphingid vision.

claim: The effect of light intensity on sphingid visual flight control has been quantified.
source: The effect of light intensity on their visual flight control has been quantified recently (Sponberg et al., 2015; Stöckl et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The crepuscular hawkmoth Manduca sexta uses information provided by antennal mechanosensors.
source: Moreover, the crepuscular hawkmoth Manduca sexta has been shown to use information provided by antennal mechanosensors, which may function similar to Dipteran halteres (Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Antennal mechanosensors in Manduca sexta may function similar to Dipteran halteres.
source: Moreover, the crepuscular hawkmoth Manduca sexta has been shown to use information provided by antennal mechanosensors, which may function similar to Dipteran halteres (Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation and comparison to haltere function.

claim: The mechanosensory Johnston's organs are present at the pedicel-flagellar joint of the antennae.
source: The mechanosensory Johnston's organs, present at the pedicel-flagellar joint of the antennae, are stimulated by deflections of the antennal flagellum, and are sensitive to a wide range of frequencies (Dieudonné et al., 2014), which far exceed the temporal response range of the visual system (Stöckl et al., 2017a; Theobald et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Johnston's organs are stimulated by deflections of the antennal flagellum.
source: The mechanosensory Johnston's organs, present at the pedicel-flagellar joint of the antennae, are stimulated by deflections of the antennal flagellum, and are sensitive to a wide range of frequencies (Dieudonné et al., 2014), which far exceed the temporal response range of the visual system (Stöckl et al., 2017a; Theobald et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to research on Johnston's organs.

claim: Johnston's organs are sensitive to a wide range of frequencies.
source: The mechanosensory Johnston's organs, present at the pedicel-flagellar joint of the antennae, are stimulated by deflections of the antennal flagellum, and are sensitive to a wide range of frequencies (Dieudonné et al., 2014), which far exceed the temporal response range of the visual system (Stöckl et al., 2017a; Theobald et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to research on Johnston's organs.

claim: The frequency range of Johnston's organs far exceeds the temporal response range of the visual system.
source: The mechanosensory Johnston's organs, present at the pedicel-flagellar joint of the antennae, are stimulated by deflections of the antennal flagellum, and are sensitive to a wide range of frequencies (Dieudonné et al., 2014), which far exceed the temporal response range of the visual system (Stöckl et al., 2017a; Theobald et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations comparing mechanosensory and visual temporal responses.

claim: After ablation of their flagella, the Johnston's organs of M. sexta no longer receive relevant information, causing flight instability.
source: After ablation of their flagella, the Johnston's organs of M. sexta no longer receive relevant information, causing flight instability in these moths, whereas re-attachment of the flagella statistically significantly improves their flight performance (Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Re-attachment of the flagella statistically significantly improves flight performance in M. sexta.
source: After ablation of their flagella, the Johnston's organs of M. sexta no longer receive relevant information, causing flight instability in these moths, whereas re-attachment of the flagella statistically significantly improves their flight performance (Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Impaired flight performance following flagellar ablation was observed in the tortoise-shell butterfly Aglais urticae.
source: Impaired flight performance following flagellar ablation was also observed in other Lepidopteran species, such as the tortoise-shell butterfly Aglais urticae (Gewecke and Niehaus, 1981; Niehaus, 1981) and the diurnal swallowtail moth Urania fulgens (Sane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Impaired flight performance following flagellar ablation was observed in the diurnal swallowtail moth Urania fulgens.
source: Impaired flight performance following flagellar ablation was also observed in other Lepidopteran species, such as the tortoise-shell butterfly Aglais urticae (Gewecke and Niehaus, 1981; Niehaus, 1981) and the diurnal swallowtail moth Urania fulgens (Sane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Macroglossum stellatarum retains both the motivation and ability to fly after flagella ablation.
source: To address these questions, we chose an insect model which retains both the motivation and ability to fly after flagella ablation: the diurnal hawkmoth Macroglossum stellatarum.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript (Table 1).

claim: M. stellatarum feed from flowers while hovering in front of them.
source: M. stellatarum feed from flowers while hovering in front of them, and previous studies have underscored the importance of visual feedback on their flower tracking behaviour (Farina et al., 1995; Farina et al., 1994; Kern, 1998; Stöckl et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about M. stellatarum behavior supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have underscored the importance of visual feedback on M. stellatarum flower tracking behaviour.
source: M. stellatarum feed from flowers while hovering in front of them, and previous studies have underscored the importance of visual feedback on their flower tracking behaviour (Farina et al., 1995; Farina et al., 1994; Kern, 1998; Stöckl et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The number of animals taking off and feeding from the flower decreased significantly with flagella ablation.
source: The number of animals taking off and feeding from the flower decreased significantly with flagella ablation, but returned to control levels following reattachment (Table 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by data presented in Table 1 and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The number of animals taking off and feeding from the flower returned to control levels following flagella reattachment.
source: The number of animals taking off and feeding from the flower decreased significantly with flagella ablation, but returned to control levels following reattachment (Table 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by data presented in Table 1 and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 60% of individuals with ablated flagella approached and fed from the flower in bright light.
source: Yet, depending on light levels, a substantial proportion of individuals with ablated flagella still approached and fed from the flower (60% in bright and 36% in dim light), making it possible to study the combined roles of vision and antennal mechanosensory feedback on flight control in more detail.
evidence: This is directly supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: 36% of individuals with ablated flagella approached and fed from the flower in dim light.
source: Yet, depending on light levels, a substantial proportion of individuals with ablated flagella still approached and fed from the flower (60% in bright and 36% in dim light), making it possible to study the combined roles of vision and antennal mechanosensory feedback on flight control in more detail.
evidence: This is directly supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Moths with ablated flagella had distinctly longer and more tortuous flight trajectories than moths in the control and flagella re-attached conditions when approaching the flower.
source: When approaching the flower, moths with ablated flagella had distinctly longer and more tortuous flight trajectories than moths in the control and flagella re-attached conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), pointing toward an impairment of flight control due to flagella ablation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ablated moths had a greater positional variation when hovering in front of the stationary flower than moths in the other two antennal conditions.
source: When hovering in front of the stationary flower, we noticed that ablated moths had a greater positional variation in relation to their target position than moths in the other two antennal conditions, as evident from their thorax position over time (blue line, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The amplitude of thoracic jitter decreased with increasing frequencies in all three antennal conditions.
source: In all three antennal conditions, the amplitude of this thoracic 'jitter' decreased with increasing frequencies (i.e. the animals performed smaller movements at higher frequencies, Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: At 3000 lux, the thoracic jitter of ablated moths was statistically significantly larger than that of the other two antennal conditions between 0.7 and 5 Hz, and between 8 and 11 Hz.
source: At 3000 lux, the thoracic jitter of ablated moths was statistically significantly larger than that of the other two antennal conditions between 0.7 and 5 Hz, and between 8 and 11 Hz (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2), whereas the difference between control and re-attached condition was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The difference in thoracic jitter between control and re-attached condition was not statistically significant.
source: At 3000 lux, the thoracic jitter of ablated moths was statistically significantly larger than that of the other two antennal conditions between 0.7 and 5 Hz, and between 8 and 11 Hz (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2), whereas the difference between control and re-attached condition was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Re-attaching the flagellum restored flight performance close to the control state.
source: Thus, re-attaching the flagellum restored flight performance close to the control state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing no significant difference between control and re-attached conditions.

claim: Many insects, including hawkmoths, use abdominal movements for aerial stabilization during flight.
source: Because many insects, including hawkmoths, use abdominal movements for aerial stabilization during flight (Camhi, 1970; Dyhr et al., 2013; Hinterwirth et al., 2012), we also quantified the movement of the abdomen over the same frequency range.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In flagella ablated moths, abdominal movement magnitude was statistically significantly larger than in control moths or flagella re-attached moths over the entire range of frequencies tested.
source: Across all three antennal conditions, the abdominal and thoracic movements revealed similar trends; in flagella ablated moths, their magnitude was statistically significantly larger than in control moths or flagella re-attached moths over the entire range of frequencies tested (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Abdominal jitter of moths with re-attached flagella was not statistically significantly different from control moths except for one frequency (1.66 Hz).
source: Like thoracic jitter, abdominal jitter of moths with re-attached flagella was not statistically significantly different from control moths (except for one frequency: 1.66 Hz).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Hovering is a dynamically unstable flight mode.
source: Since hovering is a dynamically unstable flight mode (Liang and Sun, 2013; Wu and Sun, 2012), hovering animals need continual sensory feedback to maintain a fixed position (Cowan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on hovering flight dynamics.

claim: Hovering animals need continual sensory feedback to maintain a fixed position.
source: Since hovering is a dynamically unstable flight mode (Liang and Sun, 2013; Wu and Sun, 2012), hovering animals need continual sensory feedback to maintain a fixed position (Cowan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and logical inference from the instability of hovering.

claim: Antennal mechanosensory feedback is required for the control of hovering flight.
source: Because flagella ablated moths showed larger positional jitter, especially at higher frequencies, we conclude that antennal mechanosensory feedback is required for the control of hovering flight.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased jitter in ablated moths.

claim: Without antennal input, feedback about deviations from the target position is likely supplied by the visual system and is therefore slower.
source: Without antennal input, the feedback about deviations from the target position, likely supplied by the visual system and therefore slower, causes moths to drift further from their target position before a corrective manoeuvre can be initiated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and knowledge about visual processing speeds.

claim: Without antennal input, moths drift further from their target position before a corrective manoeuvre can be initiated.
source: Without antennal input, the feedback about deviations from the target position, likely supplied by the visual system and therefore slower, causes moths to drift further from their target position before a corrective manoeuvre can be initiated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing larger positional jitter in ablated moths.

claim: Drifting further from target position results in greater thoracic and abdominal movements.
source: This in turn results in greater thoracic and abdominal movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The sum-of-sines stimulus decreased in amplitude with increasing frequency to retain a constant velocity.
source: one pattern was generated from a sum of sine-waves ranging from 0.5 to 8.9 Hz. They decreased in amplitude with increasing frequency to retain a constant velocity ('sum-of-sines', Figure 3A), which allowed the hawkmoths to track the entire stimulus successfully.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The sum-of-sines stimulus allowed the hawkmoths to track the entire stimulus successfully.
source: one pattern was generated from a sum of sine-waves ranging from 0.5 to 8.9 Hz. They decreased in amplitude with increasing frequency to retain a constant velocity ('sum-of-sines', Figure 3A), which allowed the hawkmoths to track the entire stimulus successfully.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental observations and data.

claim: The chirp stimulus had a constant amplitude while its frequency increased over time from 0 to 7.3 Hz.
source: The second movement pattern had a constant amplitude, while its frequency increased over time from 0 to 7.3 Hz over time ('chirp', Figure 1D and 3C), thus resulting in increasing flower velocity.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figures 1D and 3C.

claim: The chirp stimulus was designed to test the limits of the hawkmoths' manoeuvrability.
source: This stimulus was designed to test the limits of the hawkmoths' manoeuvrability, as the increasing velocity made it more challenging for them to track the artificial flower.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: Hawkmoths with ablated flagella often overshot the movements of the flower when tracking a moving robotic flower at 3000 lux, specifically at higher frequencies.
source: When tracking a moving robotic flower at 3000 lux, hawkmoths with ablated flagella often overshot the movements of the flower, specifically at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: With increasing frequencies, moths increasingly lagged behind the phase of flower movements more strongly.
source: With increasing frequencies, moths also increasingly lagged behind the phase of flower movements more strongly.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tracking performance of control hawkmoths with the sum-of-sines stimulus was consistent with previous investigations of intact individuals of M. stellatarum.
source: When tracking the sum-of-sines stimulus, tracking performance of control hawkmoths was consistent with previous investigations of intact individuals of this species (Farina et al., 1995; Farina et al., 1994; Stöckl et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: At 3000 lux, control moths' tracking errors were close to 0 for flower movements up to 1 Hz.
source: In all antennal conditions, the control moths tracked the sum-of-sines stimulus accurately at low flower frequencies (Figure 3A): at 3000 lux, their tracking errors were close to 0 for flower movements up to 1 Hz, indicating nearly perfect tracking (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in tracking error between antennal conditions for frequencies below 2 Hz.
source: With increasing frequency, tracking errors increased, but there was no statistically significant difference in tracking error between antennal conditions for frequencies below 2 Hz (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 4.

claim: In the flower frequency range of 2 to 5 Hz, hawkmoths with re-attached flagella had statistically significantly higher tracking errors than control moths.
source: In this flower frequency range, hawkmoths with re-attached flagella also had statistically significantly higher tracking errors than control moths.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis in Supplementary file 4.

claim: The reduction of antennal mechanosensory feedback impaired flight control specifically at the higher temporal frequencies of flower movement.
source: Thus, the reduction of antennal mechanosensory feedback impaired flight control specifically at the higher temporal frequencies of flower movement, which compelled the moths to perform faster turns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased tracking errors at higher frequencies.

claim: The ability of flagella ablated moths to track at frequencies below 2 Hz suggests that vision (and possibly other sensory modalities) provide feedback that is sufficiently fast to enable control of slower manoeuvres.
source: The ability of flagella ablated moths to track at frequencies below 2 Hz suggests that vision (and possibly other sensory modalities) provide feedback that is sufficiently fast to enable control of slower manoeuvres.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no difference in tracking at low frequencies.

claim: At low flower frequencies, hawkmoths of all antennal conditions tracked the chirp stimulus with high fidelity.
source: At low flower frequencies, hawkmoths of all antennal conditions tracked this stimulus with high fidelity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: As the flower frequency increased with the chirp stimulus, flagella ablated moths tended to overshoot the position of the flower at the end of each sideways movement.
source: However, as the flower frequency increased, flagella ablated moths tended to overshoot the position of the flower at the end of each sideways movement, when the flower movement changed direction.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The accumulated phase lag and overshoot were eventually large enough to cause ablated moths to lose contact with the nectary and abort flower tracking.
source: The accumulated phase lag and overshoot were eventually large enough to cause the moths to lose contact with the nectary and abort flower tracking (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only 1 out of 12 ablated moths succeeded in following the flower movement during the entire chirp stimulus at 3000 lux.
source: Only 1 out of 12 ablated moths succeeded in following the flower movement during the entire stimulus at 3000 lux.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: All control moths tracked the chirp stimulus until the maximum frequency.
source: In contrast, all control and 10 out of 12 re-attached moths tracked the flower until the maximum frequency.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: 10 out of 12 re-attached moths tracked the chirp stimulus until the maximum frequency.
source: In contrast, all control and 10 out of 12 re-attached moths tracked the flower until the maximum frequency.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: At 3000 lx, there was no statistically significant difference in tracking abortion frequency between the control and re-attached flagella moths.
source: At 3000 lx, there was no statistically significant difference between the control and re-attached flagella moths (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Flagella ablated hawkmoths aborted flower tracking at a median frequency of 4.4 Hz.
source: Flagella ablated hawkmoths aborted flower tracking at a median frequency of only 4.4 Hz, statistically significantly lower than the other two conditions (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Flagella ablated hawkmoths aborted flower tracking at a statistically significantly lower frequency than the other two conditions.
source: Flagella ablated hawkmoths aborted flower tracking at a median frequency of only 4.4 Hz, statistically significantly lower than the other two conditions (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Moths in all antennal conditions tracked flower movements well at low frequencies.
source: Despite the differences in the movement patterns of the two stimuli and their demands on flower tracking, we observed similar trends in hawkmoth flight performance. Moths in all antennal conditions tracked flower movements well at low frequencies, whereas flagella ablated hawkmoths were statistically significantly impaired at higher frequencies compared to the other two antennal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by data from both the sum-of-sines and chirp stimuli.

claim: Flagella ablated hawkmoths were statistically significantly impaired at higher frequencies compared to the other two antennal conditions.
source: Despite the differences in the movement patterns of the two stimuli and their demands on flower tracking, we observed similar trends in hawkmoth flight performance. Moths in all antennal conditions tracked flower movements well at low frequencies, whereas flagella ablated hawkmoths were statistically significantly impaired at higher frequencies compared to the other two antennal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by data from both the sum-of-sines and chirp stimuli.

claim: The average flower frequency at which ablated moths failed to track the chirp stimulus was consistent with the frequency range for which the tracking error with the sum-of-sines-stimulus was greatest.
source: The average flower frequency at which ablated moths failed to track the chirp stimulus was consistent with the frequency range for which the tracking error with the sum-of-sines-stimulus was greatest, despite the difference in flower velocity between stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing data from the two different stimuli.

claim: Antennal feedback is crucial for fast turns or directional changes which are associated with changes in body posture.
source: These data show that antennal feedback is crucial for fast turns - or directional changes - which are associated with changes in body posture.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing impairments at higher frequencies.

claim: Hawkmoths of all antennal conditions did not differ in their flight performance when performing slower movements.
source: In the experiments described so far, hawkmoths of all antennal conditions did not differ in their flight performance when performing slower movements (at lower frequencies of positional jitter when hovering at a stationary flower, and at flower frequencies when tracking a moving flower).
evidence: This is supported by data showing no significant differences at low frequencies.

claim: At slower movement frequencies, feedback from other sensory modalities likely mitigated the problems in flight control caused by antennal ablation.
source: At these movement frequencies, feedback from other sensory modalities likely mitigated the problems in flight control caused by antennal ablation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ablated moths performed similarly to control moths at low frequencies.

claim: Visual feedback is known to provide information about changes in insect body (head) position in flight.
source: In particular, visual feedback is known to provide information about changes in insect body (head) position in flight (for a review see Srinivasan et al., 1999), albeit with longer latencies and a lower frequency range than mechanosensory feedback (Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Visual feedback has longer latencies and a lower frequency range than mechanosensory feedback.
source: In particular, visual feedback is known to provide information about changes in insect body (head) position in flight (for a review see Srinivasan et al., 1999), albeit with longer latencies and a lower frequency range than mechanosensory feedback (Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The latency of visual feedback depends on the ambient light intensity.
source: Because the latency of visual feedback depends on the ambient light intensity (Stöckl et al., 2017a), we next tested how the reliability of visual feedback affected the hawkmoth's flight performance by decreasing the ambient light intensity in combination with the antennal manipulations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The same group of hawkmoths was tested at an illumination of 30 lux, close to the light intensity limit at which these diurnal hawkmoths are still able to reliably approach and feed from the artificial flowers.
source: We tested the same group of hawkmoths at an illumination of 30 lux, close to the light intensity limit at which these diurnal hawkmoths are still able to reliably approach and feed from the artificial flowers (Stöckl et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design supported by a citation.

claim: In dim light, the low speed and reduced reliability of the visual input to flight control causes larger tracking errors when flowers move at high frequencies for all antennal conditions.
source: In dim light, the low speed and reduced reliability of the visual input to flight control causes larger tracking errors when flowers move at high frequencies for all antennal conditions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Visual input is essential for moths to identify and track the flower movement relative to their own position.
source: This effect is explained by the fact that visual input is essential for moths to identify and track the flower movement relative to their own position – antennal mechanosensors cannot provide the required information (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional roles of vision and mechanosensation.

claim: Antennal mechanosensors cannot provide information about flower movement relative to the moth's own position.
source: This effect is explained by the fact that visual input is essential for moths to identify and track the flower movement relative to their own position – antennal mechanosensors cannot provide the required information (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional roles of vision and mechanosensation.

claim: Because visual processing is slower in dim light, moths face greater difficulties in resolving fast flower movements, which causes failure in tracking.
source: Because visual processing is slower in dim light, moths face greater difficulties in resolving fast flower movements, which causes failure in tracking (Sponberg et al., 2015; Stöckl et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There was no specific effect of light intensity on flight control in the flagella ablated moths.
source: We did not observe a specific effect of light intensity on flight control in the flagella ablated moths.
evidence: This is supported by data showing similar light intensity effects across all antennal conditions.

claim: Visual feedback is unable to mitigate the instability caused by the loss of antennal mechanosensory feedback even at higher resolution under brightly lit conditions.
source: This suggests that, even at higher resolution under brightly lit conditions, visual feedback is unable to mitigate the instability caused by the loss of antennal mechanosensory feedback.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of interaction between light intensity and antennal condition.

claim: Recent recordings of descending neurons in Oleander hawkmoth show that they respond to both visual and mechanosensory stimulation.
source: This is unlikely, as recent recordings of descending neurons in Oleander hawkmoth show that they respond to both visual and mechanosensory stimulation (Mohan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Mechanosensors in Johnston's organ respond to antennal displacements at frequencies of up to 100 Hz in the hawkmoth M. sexta.
source: The latter hypothesis is consistent with physiological studies showing that mechanosensors in Johnston's organ respond to antennal displacements at frequencies of up to 100 Hz in the hawkmoth M. sexta (Sane et al., 2007), whereas the wide-field motion-sensitive neurons of the same species cease to respond at temporal frequencies above 20 Hz (Stöckl et al., 2017a), at which most mechanosensors of the Johnston's organ only show a weak response.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to physiological research.

claim: The wide-field motion-sensitive neurons of M. sexta cease to respond at temporal frequencies above 20 Hz.
source: The latter hypothesis is consistent with physiological studies showing that mechanosensors in Johnston's organ respond to antennal displacements at frequencies of up to 100 Hz in the hawkmoth M. sexta (Sane et al., 2007), whereas the wide-field motion-sensitive neurons of the same species cease to respond at temporal frequencies above 20 Hz (Stöckl et al., 2017a), at which most mechanosensors of the Johnston's organ only show a weak response.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to physiological research.

claim: At temporal frequencies above 20 Hz, most mechanosensors of the Johnston's organ only show a weak response.
source: The latter hypothesis is consistent with physiological studies showing that mechanosensors in Johnston's organ respond to antennal displacements at frequencies of up to 100 Hz in the hawkmoth M. sexta (Sane et al., 2007), whereas the wide-field motion-sensitive neurons of the same species cease to respond at temporal frequencies above 20 Hz (Stöckl et al., 2017a), at which most mechanosensors of the Johnston's organ only show a weak response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited physiological data.

claim: In M. stellatarum, mechanosensory feedback from antennae is required for the control of fast flight manoeuvres and rapid deviations from their hovering position.
source: We showed here that in the diurnal hawkmoth M. stellatarum, mechanosesory feedback from antennae is required for the control of fast flight manoeuvres and rapid deviations from their hovering position, whereas their visual system drives the control of slower manoeuvres.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: The visual system of M. stellatarum drives the control of slower manoeuvres.
source: We showed here that in the diurnal hawkmoth M. stellatarum, mechanosesory feedback from antennae is required for the control of fast flight manoeuvres and rapid deviations from their hovering position, whereas their visual system drives the control of slower manoeuvres.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: These findings detail a striking similarity to the interaction between mechanosensory halteres and vision in the Dipteran flight control model.
source: These findings detail a striking similarity to the interaction between mechanosensory halteres and vision in the Dipteran flight control model, and for the first time dissect the combined role of visual and antennal mechanosensory feeback for flight control in hawkmoths, which may be representative for many other non-Dipteran insects.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the findings to previous research on Dipteran flight control.

claim: Wild adult Macroglossum stellatarum were caught in Sorède, France.
source: Wild adult Macroglossum stellatarum L. (Sphingidae), were caught in Sorède, France.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used to obtain study animals.

claim: Eggs were collected and the caterpillars raised on their native host plant Gallium sp.
source: Eggs were collected and the caterpillars raised on their native host plant Gallium sp.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used to rear study animals.

claim: All animals were tested with intact antennae first (control), then with ablated flagella (ablated), and finally with re-attached flagella (reattach).
source: All animals were tested with intact antennae first (control), then with ablated flagella (ablated), and finally with re-attached flagella (reattach) as described below (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Only data from animals that could be tested under all three antennal conditions was included in the final data analysis.
source: Only data from animals that could be tested under all three antennal conditions was included in the final data analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis criteria.

claim: For flagella ablation, flagella were clipped with a pair of surgical scissors, while retaining 5–10 annuli.
source: For flagella ablation, moths were held, by their thorax under a dissection microscope and their flagella were clipped with a pair of surgical scissors, while retaining 5–10 annuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical methods.

claim: Retaining 5–10 annuli ensured that Johnston's organs, located at the base of the antennae, were left intact but unloaded.
source: This ensured that Johnston's organs, located at the base of the antennae, were left intact but unloaded.
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for the surgical method.

claim: Dry flagella had statistically significantly lower weights than freshly ablated flagella.
source: Dry flagella had statistically significantly lower weights than freshly ablated flagella (moist: 1.2 ± 0.2 mg, dry: 0.4 ± 0.3 mg; median and inter-quartile range, Wilcoxon rank sum test, z-value = −5.915, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The average head:antenna weight ratio was 3.38:1 ± 0.68 standard deviation.
source: The resulting average head:antenna ratio was 3.38:1 ± 0.68 standard deviation, with a weight of 10.5 ± 1.4 mg for the head and 3.1 ± 0.31 mg for the two antennae.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The animals weighed an average of 252 ± 66 mg.
source: The animals weighed an average of 252 ± 66 mg.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: With the sum-of-sines stimulus at 3000 lux, hawkmoths in the control condition showed a phase lag of approximately 90° at the highest temporal frequency of 8.9 Hz, suggesting a response delay of less than 30 ms.
source: with the sum-of-sines stimulus at 3000 lux, hawkmoths in the control condition showed a phase lag of approximately 90° at the highest temporal frequency of 8.9 Hz (Figure 3—figure supplements 1,2), suggesting a response delay of less than 30 ms.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1,2.

claim: The phase delay with the chirp stimulus at 6.5 Hz in the control condition at 3000 lux was close to 80°, indicating a response delay of 35 ms.
source: Similarly, the phase delay with the chirp stimulus at 6.5 Hz in the control condition at 3000 lux was close to 80° (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating a response delay of 35 ms.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fastest latencies of wide-field motion neurons in blowflies are approximately 25 ms.
source: Considering that visually tracking the flower likely involves computing a directional motion component, and the fastest latencies of wide-field motion neurons in blowflies are approximately 25 ms (Warzecha and Egelhaaf, 2000), it is unlikely that such fast flower tracking responses are purely elicited by vision in M. stellatarum.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to physiological research.

claim: It is unlikely that such fast flower tracking responses are purely elicited by vision in M. stellatarum.
source: Considering that visually tracking the flower likely involves computing a directional motion component, and the fastest latencies of wide-field motion neurons in blowflies are approximately 25 ms (Warzecha and Egelhaaf, 2000), it is unlikely that such fast flower tracking responses are purely elicited by vision in M. stellatarum.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the observed response delays to known visual processing speeds.

claim: Recent work by Roth et al. (2016) in Manduca sexta has demonstrated that mechanoreceptors on the proboscis can play a role in monitoring flower position, in addition to visual input.
source: Recent work by Roth et al. (2016) in Manduca sexta has demonstrated that mechanoreceptors on the proboscis can play a role in monitoring flower position, in addition to visual input.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The phase lags observed in M. sexta for purely mechanosensory tracking are distinctly larger than the ones observed for flower tracking in the current experiments.
source: We cannot exclude a mechansensory component to flower tracking originating from the proboscis in M. stellatarum, but the phase lags observed in M. sexta for purely mechanosensory tracking, even though shorter than those for purely visual tracking at higher temporal frequencies, are still distinctly larger than the ones observed for flower tracking in our experiments (Roth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to data from a cited study.

claim: The flowertracking responses of the hawkmoths might include mechanical coupling between the head and the flower via the proboscis.
source: Another possible explanation for the short tracking delays at high frequencies is a direct mechanical coupling between the head of the hawkmoth and the flower via the proboscis. The flowertracking responses of the hawkmoths might include this mechanical coupling, which could explain their extraordinarily fast responses at high flower movement frequencies.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: The change in responses across antennal conditions and light intensities shows that there is a strong sensorimotor component of the behaviour.
source: The change in responses across antennal conditions and light intensities shows that there is, nevertheless, a strong sensorimotor component of the behaviour, and since the potential mechanical coupling, as well as putative mechanosensory input from the proboscis, were present in all antennal conditions as well as light intensities, they did not affect the observed results with respect to visual and antennal mechanosensory feedback.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and results.

claim: Changes in flight performance were observed upon antennal ablation and re-attachement both during flower approach and hovering at stationary flowers.
source: Moreover, we did observe changes in flight performance upon antennal ablation and re-attachement both during flower approach (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and hovering at stationary flowers (Figure 2, Figure 4C,D), where mechanosensory inputs and mechanical coupling did not play a role.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback from the antennae is essential for the control of fast flight manoeuvres, which require corrective movements to occur in timescales that may not be sufficient for the transduction of visual feedback.
source: Thus, we conclude that mechanosensory feedback from the antennae is essential for the control of fast flight manoeuvres, which require corrective movements to occur in timescales that may not be sufficient for the transduction of visual feedback.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and analysis.

claim: The control of fast saccadic rotations in Dipterans mainly requires mechanosensory feedback from the halteres, while vision plays a relatively marginal role.
source: This again is analogous to the finding that the control of fast saccadic rotations in Dipterans mainly requires mechanosensory feedback from the halteres, while vision plays a relatively marginal role (Bender and Dickinson, 2006; Sherman and Dickinson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Dipteran flight control.

claim: In Dipteran flies, vision and haltere mechanosensation operate in complementary frequency ranges.
source: In Dipteran flies, vision and haltere mechanosensation operate in complementary frequency ranges, and while both inputs are required for stable flight under most circumstances (Yarger and Fox, 2016), they do not seem to compensate for each other (Mureli and Fox, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Dipteran flies, vision and haltere mechanosensation do not seem to compensate for each other.
source: In Dipteran flies, vision and haltere mechanosensation operate in complementary frequency ranges, and while both inputs are required for stable flight under most circumstances (Yarger and Fox, 2016), they do not seem to compensate for each other (Mureli and Fox, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In honeybees, airflow on the antennae and optic flow influence antennal positioning in tethered as well as free flight.
source: For example, in honeybees, airflow on the antennae and optic flow influence antennal positioning in tethered as well as free flight (Roy Khurana and Sane, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the Oleander hawkmoth Daphnis nerii, visual feedback modulates antennal positioning.
source: In the Oleander hawkmoth Daphnis nerii, visual feedback modulates antennal positioning in a similar way (Krishnan and Sane, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Visual input is essential for moths to identify and track the flower movement relative to their own position.
source: This effect is explained by the fact that visual input is essential for moths to identify and track the flower movement relative to their own position – antennal mechanosensors cannot provide the required information (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional roles of the sensory systems.

claim: Recent recordings of descending neurons in Oleander hawkmoth show that they respond to both visual and mechanosensory stimulation.
source: This is unlikely, as recent recordings of descending neurons in Oleander hawkmoth show that they respond to both visual and mechanosensory stimulation (Mohan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Vision and mechanosensation may share descending pathways but operate in different frequency ranges.
source: Alternatively, vision and mechanosensation share descending pathways but operate in different frequency ranges, and the visual input is too slow to compensate for the lack of antennal mechanosensory feedback.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental findings.

claim: The visual input is too slow to compensate for the lack of antennal mechanosensory feedback.
source: Alternatively, vision and mechanosensation share descending pathways but operate in different frequency ranges, and the visual input is too slow to compensate for the lack of antennal mechanosensory feedback.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing no compensation.

claim: Antennal mechanosensation represents one strategy for flying insects to obtain rapid sensory feedback about changes in self-motion, which is crucial for flight control.
source: Antennal mechanosensation represents one strategy for flying insects to obtain rapid sensory feedback about changes in self-motion, which is crucial for flight control.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and broader context.

claim: In M. stellatarum, mechanosensory feedback from antennae is required for the control of fast flight manoeuvres and rapid deviations from their hovering position.
source: We showed here that in the diurnal hawkmoth M. stellatarum, mechanosesory feedback from antennae is required for the control of fast flight manoeuvres and rapid deviations from their hovering position, whereas their visual system drives the control of slower manoeuvres.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: The visual system of M. stellatarum drives the control of slower manoeuvres.
source: We showed here that in the diurnal hawkmoth M. stellatarum, mechanosesory feedback from antennae is required for the control of fast flight manoeuvres and rapid deviations from their hovering position, whereas their visual system drives the control of slower manoeuvres.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: These findings may be representative for many other non-Dipteran insects.
source: These findings detail a striking similarity to the interaction between mechanosensory halteres and vision in the Dipteran flight control model, and for the first time dissect the combined role of visual and antennal mechanosensory feeback for flight control in hawkmoths, which may be representative for many other non-Dipteran insects.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Flagellar re-attachment improved flight performance by reloading the Johnston's organs, both for stationary hovering and flower-tracking behaviors.
source: As also observed in previous experiments by Sane et al. (2007), re-attaching the flagellum restored flight performance by reloading the Johnston's organs, both for stationary hovering and flower-tracking behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and comparison to previous research.

claim: This is consistent with the growing body of evidence that Lepidoptera use antennal Johnston's organs for flight control.
source: This is consistent with the growing body of evidence (Dieudonné et al., 2014; Gewecke and Niehaus, 1981; Niehaus, 1981; Sane et al., 2010) that Lepidoptera use antennal Johnston's organs for flight control.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Hymenopteran insects (Polistes humilis) seem to purely rely on visual information to stabilise their head during roll manoeuvres.
source: While Hymenopteran insects (Polistes humilis) seem to purely rely on visual information to stabilise their head during roll manoeuvres (Viollet and Zeil, 2013), preliminary data from hawkmoths shows that they might require antennal feedback for head stabilisation (Sane et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Preliminary data from hawkmoths shows that they might require antennal feedback for head stabilisation.
source: While Hymenopteran insects (Polistes humilis) seem to purely rely on visual information to stabilise their head during roll manoeuvres (Viollet and Zeil, 2013), preliminary data from hawkmoths shows that they might require antennal feedback for head stabilisation (Sane et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to preliminary research.

claim: Flagella re-attachment did not entirely restore flight performance back to the levels of intact animals.
source: These differences between experimental conditions suggest that flagella re-attachement did not entirely restore flight performance back to the levels of intact animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical differences observed between re-attached and control conditions.

claim: Re-attached flagella were not connected to the haemolymph system of the hawkmoth and thus dried out, which reduced their weight by more than 50%.
source: One reason for this might be that some properties of the re-attached flagella differed from those of intact animals. Re-attached flagella were not connected to the haemolymph system of the hawkmoth and thus dried out, which reduced their weight by more than 50% (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements described in the Materials and methods.

claim: Changes in weight may considerably alter the sensory input to the Johnston's organs.
source: Since the flagella are thought to provide a mass that inertial forces act on (Sane et al., 2007), changes in weight may considerably alter the sensory input to the Johnston's organs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known function of flagella and the observed weight changes.

claim: There are mechanosensors along the length of the flagellum, which may be important for flight control.
source: Moreover, there are also mechanosensors along the length of the flagellum, which may be important for flight control.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: When the antennal nerve is severed, these mechanosensory units remain inactive even after flagellar reattachment.
source: When the antennal nerve is severed, these mechanosensory units remain inactive even after flagellar reattachment, which may add to the observed deterioration in their ability to control flight.
evidence: This is an inference based on the surgical procedure and known neurophysiology.

claim: Control of slower manoeuvres is not as dependent on antennal mechanosensory feedback, as is the control of faster manoeuvres.
source: This suggests that control of slower manoeuvres is not as dependent on antennal mechanosensory feedback, as is the control of faster manoeuvres.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no difference at low frequencies.

claim: Flagella ablated hawkmoths performed statistically significantly worse than moths with intact and re-attached flagella at flower movements above 2 Hz.
source: On the other hand, flagella ablated hawkmoths performed statistically significantly worse than moths with intact and re-attached flagella at flower movements above 2 Hz, where more rapid turns are required to follow the lateral trajectory of the moving flower.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Slower rotations of fruit flies are tuned stronger to visual feedback, whereas faster rotations require feedback from haltere mechanosensors.
source: Our findings are mirrored in the study of Dipteran flight control: slower rotations of fruit flies are tuned stronger to visual feedback, whereas faster rotations require feedback from haltere mechanosensors (Sherman and Dickinson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on Dipteran flight control.
